1:
Who is addressed is disputed three ways. Henry takes the rich for "the worldly and unbelieving Jews", noting that the epistle is directed not to brethren in Christ but to the twelve tribes, and that these are the men said to condemn and kill the just, "which the Christians had no power to do": "they would not hear the word, and therefore it is written, that they might read it." Calvin denies it: "there is nothing said that can lead to such an opinion", since the two preceding chapters were addressed to believers and "the sins here condemned are not worse than those previously condemned"; Peter and Jude show professors of that day "not a whit better than many who profess religion in our age." Gill agrees, restricting it to men within the church who were "not rich towards God", neither all rich men nor the openly profane. Barnes rejects both: an unbelieving readership is improbable because James can hardly have supposed his letter would reach them, a believing one because "it can hardly be supposed that men were tolerated in the church, in the times of the apostles, who were guilty of the oppressions" described. His own reading makes the address rhetorical — written "not perhaps expecting that they would see what he had written", but to set the wrongs before the poor who suffered them. Robertson takes the rich simply as a class, believer or unbeliever, finding here "a certain grim comfort in the hardships of poverty".

Whether any door is left open divides Calvin from Ellicott. Calvin holds that "they are mistaken who consider that James here exhorts the rich to repentance": it is "a simple denunciation of God's judgment... for all that he says tends only to despair" — and he argues it from the verb, since "repentance has indeed its weeping, but being mixed with consolation, it does not proceed to howling." Henry reads the imperative so too: "it is not said, Weep and repent, for this the apostle does not expect from them." Ellicott answers Calvin by name, urging that "all prophecy, whether evil or good, is conditional", so no irrevocable doom was pronounced by "a Christian Jeremiah".

The howling draws the philologists. Robertson calls it an old onomatopoetic verb found only here in the New Testament and renders the pair "burst into weeping, howling with grief"; Ellicott traces it through the Greek of Isaiah 13:6, "a picture word, imitating the cry of anguish". On what the misery is they largely agree. Clarke thinks James "seems here to assume the very air and character of a prophet", foretelling desolation "not only in Judea, but in all the provinces where they sojourned"; Wesley dates the letter shortly before the siege of Jerusalem and calls those calamities "an awful prelude of that wrath which was to fall upon them in the world to come"; Ellicott takes secondary references with the primary one to Jerusalem.

The corrupting of verse 2 turns on what ancient wealth was. Clarke insists the word cannot mean gold or silver, "for these could not putrefy", but the produce of fields and flocks; Wesley and Barnes agree, Barnes adding that such stores were laid against famine. Robertson notes the verb is intransitive — the wealth "has rotted" — and that the compound for moth-eaten occurs only here, at Job 13:28 and in the Sibylline Oracles: "rich robes as heirlooms, but moth-eaten." Calvin weighs two senses and prefers the harsher: not that riches are fading, but that these men retained "everything they could lay hold on, that it might rot uselessly in their chests" — "what God had created for the use of men, they destroyed, as though they were the enemies of mankind." The vices, he adds, are not all found in the same men: "such is the malignity of some, that they grudge to others the common sun and air."
3:
Whether gold can rust is answered four ways. Gill grants that "in length of time gold and silver will change, and contract a rustiness". Barnes concedes the chemistry and rescues the text: the metals do not properly oxidise, but kept long in a damp place "they will contract a dark colour, resembling rust in appearance", and there is anyway "no reason to suppose that the word was then used in the strict chemical sense". Ellicott locates the corrosion elsewhere: "the precious metals themselves do not corrode, but the base alloy does, which has been mixed with them for worldly use." Robertson denies the premise: "silver does corrode and gold will tarnish." Ellicott takes the rust as witness "not merely against, but convincing yourselves in the day of judgment"; Robertson, granting "to you" would make sense, holds "against" to be the idea.

Clarke reads the fire forward by a textual route: the Syriac drops the "as" and carries it into the next clause, yielding "ye have treasured up Fire against the last days" — not stores of corn and wine but "a magazine of fire, that shall burn up your city." Calvin takes the rust itself as the occasion of wrath, since God "has not appointed gold for rust, nor garments for moths" but designed them as helps to human life: "even spending without benefit is a witness of inhumanity".

What "the last days" names divides them flatly. Clarke insists "we are not to understand the day of judgment, but the last days of the Jewish commonwealth". Calvin insists the opposite, that the phrase means the days of the gospel and points to the judgment, and that the reference some make "to the destruction of Jerusalem, has nothing in the passage to favor it": the rich were treasuring wrath, as at Romans 2:5. Barnes takes it of the judgment; Wesley reads the treasuring as irony, laid up "when it is too late; when you have no time to enjoy them". Ellicott takes a third road, making them "the days of grace, given you for repentance", and defends James, Paul and John against the charge of expecting the end too soon: there was no mistake, only "the potential nearness of Christ"; "nought retards Christ's Second Coming so much as the false and feeble Christianity which prays 'Thy kingdom come' in frequent words."

On the withheld wages they reach for the law and then for their own century. Clarke and Ellicott both cite Leviticus 19:13 and Malachi 3:5, which forbid holding a labourer's hire overnight; Clarke adds a rabbinic parallel catching the same image: "when a poor man does any work in a house, the vapor proceeding from him, through the severity of his work, ascends towards heaven. Wo to his employer if he delay to pay him his wages." Ellicott turns the remonstrance on his own contemporaries, "a swift witness also against the like-minded of this generation, whose God is self, whose religion political economy, and whose one great object in life is to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest: as if for these ignoble purposes the Lord God had given them a brain and a soul."

Barnes devotes most of his comment to slavery, the case he takes the verse to fit best. Since the owner keeps what the slave produces beyond his maintenance, and would keep no slave if he had to pay what a freeman would bargain for, "the very essence of slavery is fraud"; were the wage fairly paid, "slavery could not live a day". His test is the Bible: slaveholders will not put it into slaves' hands, and "a system which cannot survive the most full and free circulation of the sacred Scriptures, must be founded in wrong." Ellicott repeats Bede's remark that James names the Lord of hosts "to terrify those who suppose that the poor have no helpers."
5:
Barnes stops to rescue an English word. "Been wanton" now suggests "a sense which is not in the original", the lewd and lascivious, whereas the term was "formerly used in the sense of sportive, joyous, gay", and the Greek means only to live luxuriously. Clarke goes the other way without hesitation: "ye have lived lasciviously. Ye have indulged all your sinful and sensual appetites to the uttermost; and your lives have been scandalous." Robertson keeps to the lexicon, a late and rare verb for living voluptuously. Calvin, granting that the Lord allows men to live freely on what they have, still insists that "profusion ought to be avoided and frugality practiced", recalling the prophets against those who slept on beds of ivory. He declines to make the charge universal, some rich men starving amid plenty: "the poets have imagined Tantalus to be hungry near a table well furnished. There have ever been Tantalians in the world."

"As in a day of slaughter" is read three ways. Barnes reports one rendering that has them feeding "like beasts in the day of slaughter, without care or forethought", and another that makes it a festival; he prefers a third, that they had fattened themselves as animals are fattened for killing, and "seem to live only with reference to the day of slaughter". Clarke, Calvin and Wesley take the festival sense, Clarke noting that many turned "a holy ordinance into a riotous festival". Robertson keeps the stall-fed image and calls it "consummate sarcasm on the folly of sinful rich people". Ellicott alone questions the text: the comparative "as" is an insertion, and the charge is heavier without it — they nourished their hearts in a day of slaughter, feasting while others died. Under Titus, he adds, "they themselves were the victims".

Who "the just" is divides them. Gill denies it is Christ, since James writes to professors of religion and not to the Jerusalem council, and takes it of poor saints condemned in rash judgments or dragged before the rich. Clarke agrees that "the structure of the sentence, and the connection in which it stands" require the righteous in general, who had none to plead for them. Calvin concedes the reading is true of Christ but rejects it here on a precise ground: "the death of Christ is not ascribed to the rich, but to the elders and chief priests", the singular being James's habit for the plural. Barnes leaves it undetermined. Robertson takes the article as generic, with "probably no direct reference to one individual, though it does picture well the death of Christ and also the coming death of James himself". Ellicott keeps the reference to Christ and widens it: all wrong tends towards the murder of the Just One. He then notes what Robertson only glances at — that in this verse "James the Just prophetically described his own murderers." Wesley holds both senses at once — "many just men; in particular, that Just One" — adding that they afterwards killed James.

The closing clause is left open by nearly everyone. Barnes canvasses three constructions — that God does not oppose them, that it is a question implying he will, and that the just man cannot resist — preferring the last. Robertson sets out both readings and refuses to choose: without a question mark it pictures the unresisting victim, with one it makes God the subject and the last judgment the answer — "there is no way to decide definitely." Calvin takes the just man's silence as duty and helplessness together — he ought patiently to endure, but also "he was unprotected and without any help from men". Ellicott hears the pattern of martyrdom: "the servant of the Lord must not strive" even in death. Wesley alone turns it into irony against the oppressors: "he doth not resist you — and therefore you are secure. But the Lord cometh quickly."
7:
Gill notices whom the address turns to: the poor are called brethren, "of whom he was not ashamed", where the rich got no such title "though professors of the same religion". Robertson defines the imperative by its parts — of long spirit, not losing heart — and puts it as advice to a runner: "catch your wind for a long race". Calvin reads the whole preceding denunciation as existing for this moment, since what was said against the rich "pertains to the consolation of those exposed to their wrongs with impunity": the world's present confusion "will not be perpetual".

What "the coming of the Lord" means is the chapter's most consequential dispute. Clarke has no doubt it is the fall of Jerusalem: Christ "is already on his way to destroy this wicked people, to raze their city and temple, and to destroy their polity for ever". Calvin allows that the day of the Lord elsewhere covers every manifestation of judgment and grace, "yet I prefer to regard the expression here as referring to our final deliverance". Robertson says flatly that the second coming is meant, then asks the awkward question himself: "how near or nigh did James mean? Clearly, it could only be a hope, for Jesus had distinctly said that no one knew when he would return." Barnes canvasses judgment, the end of the Jewish system and death alike, settling on the destruction of Jerusalem as most natural, the letter being written some ten or twelve years before it and ending the system of types and sacrifices. Wesley holds both: the coming is "to destroy Jerusalem", and "so is his last coming to the eye of a believer".

The husbandman is expounded with care by all of them. Calvin presses the image furthest: the farmer "suffers his life, so precious to him, to lie long deposited in the bosom of the earth, and calmly suspends his desire to gather the fruit". Henry turns it into a question — "consider him that waits for a crop of corn; and will not you wait for a crown of glory?" — and answers the complaint of delay by scale: "men count time long, because they measure it by their own lives; but all time is as nothing to God."

The two rains draw out the geographers. Clarke dates them to early November after sowing and late April as the ears fill, and notes that though promised at Deuteronomy 11:14 they had to be prayed for. Robertson notes the word for rain "is absent from the best MSS"; Ellicott answers that it "was always intended". Barnes registers a difficulty honestly: in Palestine now there are no distinct rainy seasons but one continuous wet period, so that "unless there has been some change in the climate since the times of the New Testament", the two rains must mean the first showers of autumn and the last of spring. Calvin takes both seasons as making one point, that husbandmen "are not disheartened by the slow progress of time, but bear with the delay".

On establishing the heart they converge but differ in temper. Barnes takes it of purpose and faith held unwavering; Clarke reads courage, "do not sink under your trials"; Ellicott would prefer "comfort" if it had kept its older strength, the sense being to strengthen rather than console. Calvin explains why the instruction is needed: the objection that deliverance is delayed arises because "we are too tender and delicate", and that softness is corrected by hope, "as it were by a realizing view of the near approach of our Lord". Ellicott ends on a paradox: all Christians "are citizens of a patient kingdom", whose King "is more patient, as He hath greater need of patience than His subjects, and He is patient, because He is strong. Impatience is a sign of weakness. God can afford to wait, for His time is eternity."
9:
What verse 9 forbids is read three ways, and the English word is part of the trouble. Ellicott notes that "grudge" has "curiously changed its meaning from an outward murmur to an inward feeling", preferring "murmur not". Gill keeps the inward sense, repining secretly at another's happiness. Barnes, Robertson and Clarke take it of audible grumbling, Barnes finding the idea to be fretfulness: men of "a sour, dissatisfied, discontented temper" who complain not because they are injured but because others seem weak and foolish — a spirit he calls "the offspring of pride". Calvin rejects the envy reading by name — some explain it as bidding each be contented with his own lot, "but I take another view" — and makes it an accusing groan, "when one expostulates with the Lord against another": since no one has injured nobody, universal complaint would mean universal condemnation, and "let no one ask for vengeance on others, except he wishes to bring it on his own head."

Ellicott and Robertson correct the following clause to "lest ye be judged", the words of the Sermon on the Mount. On the judge at the door the readings differ in mood. Barnes has him so near "that he can hear all that you say", Wesley "hearing every word, marking every thought", Clarke already "entering into judgment with your oppressors". Calvin makes the nearness a bridle rather than a threat: because we profane God's name by appealing to his judgment over the slightest offences, "nothing is a fitter bridle to check our rashness, than to consider that our imprecations vanish not into air." Ellicott sets the scene against the door of Revelation 3, where Christ lingers in mercy, and adds a detail from James's own death: among the mocking questions put to him was "which is the door of Jesus?" — and failing of an answer they said, "let us stone this James the Just."

The prophets are proposed as an example; Calvin is careful what kind. The comfort is not the proverb that the miserable want companions in misery — when Job's friends asked "turn to the saints, can you find any like to thee?" that "was the voice of Satan", meant to drive him to despair. James instead names men "a fellowship with whom is blessed": in our troubles we are "without judgment, being influenced by grief", seeing nothing "under a foggy sky and in the midst of storms", and must "cast our eyes to another quarter, where the sky is in a manner serene and bright". Barnes states it in two steps: if prophets were persecuted others may expect it, and their patience is a model. Ellicott fills the roll from Hebrews and concludes that James "was not advocating a religion alien to that of Moses". Wesley notes the irony that men who gloried in having prophets could not bear their message.

"The end of the Lord" produces the tile's real dispute. Barnes reports that Augustine, Luther and Wetstein took it for the death of Christ, and refuses that on two grounds: the Greek word never denotes death but termination, issue or purpose; and it would not square with what follows, since what was seen is that the Lord is very pitiful — not the prominent trait of the crucifixion, and not the virtue James is recommending. Clarke and Gill take it as Barnes does, of the issue to which God brought Job's trials, Clarke adding that "this was God's end with respect to him; but the devil's end was to drive him to despair", and observing that citing Job at all shows him "to have been a real person; for a fictitious person would not have been produced as an example". Ellicott closes by measuring the verse against Solon, who called no man happy on earth but "cried sadly, 'Look to the end'" — where James counts blessed the men who endure.
12:
Whether the verse belongs here is disputed first. Clarke is blunt — "what relation this exhortation can have to the subject in question, I confess I cannot see" — and takes it for separate advice. Robertson agrees there is "no connection with what immediately precedes", though "it is not out of place here". Gill supplies the link the others miss: as impatience should not show itself in sighs and murmurings, "so more especially it should not break forth in rash oaths". Henry reports a narrower reading, that the prohibition is against swearing at persecutors in the heat of injury, and refuses to stop there: "the apostle's warning extends to other occasions as well as this".

What is actually forbidden divides them along confessional lines; Ellicott states it most fully. The text as it stands "would support the views of the Essenes, and many of the Paulicians", and might be urged as forcibly by the Moravians or the Quakers. He gives Huther's contrary argument in fairness: swearing by God's name is nowhere mentioned here, and had James meant to forbid it "he would most certainly have mentioned it expressly", since the Law commands it. Ellicott's own conclusion rests on Christ answering Caiaphas: with the Articles, "a man may swear, when the magistrate requireth, in a cause of faith and charity". Calvin reaches the same place and names his opponents: "the Anabaptists, building on this passage, condemn all oaths, but they only shew their ignorance", since neither Christ nor James speaks of oaths in general — had the question been oaths in themselves, "to what purpose were these forms mentioned?" Gill and Wesley concur, Gill that an oath in God's name is lawful, Wesley that James "does not forbid the taking a solemn oath before a magistrate".

What the evasion consisted in they describe alike. Calvin diagnoses the motive: men think they may swear with impunity provided the divine name is not mentioned, but the pretence fails because "the glory of God is everywhere inscribed", so that naming heaven and earth designates the Worker by his works. Robertson says the Jews "split hairs in their use of profanity, and by avoiding God's name imagine that they were not really guilty of this sin, just as professing Christians today use 'pious oaths'". Clarke supplies the rabbinic rule — Akiba taught that "a man might swear with his lips, and annul it in his heart" — and Ellicott the consequence, that among so many subtle distinctions "the unlucky foreigner who trusted in an apparently firm one, too often found out his mistake".

Clarke alone presses a variant that changes the penalty. Several manuscripts join the last two words and prefix a preposition, yielding not "lest ye fall under judgment" but "lest ye fall into hypocrisy" — supported, he says, by "a great number of excellent MSS., some versions, and some of the most eminent of the fathers" — and he prefers it because it names the disease of mental reservation. Robertson and Ellicott, keeping the received text, correct the English: the word is judgment, "the act of judging rather than the judgment rendered", not condemnation.

On the remedy they converge. Barnes wants "a simple affirmation, unaccompanied by any oath or appeal to God or to any of his works", since "a man who makes that his common method of speech is the man who will be believed". Wesley says the same negatively — "let your word stand firm" — and Clarke turns it inward: "do not pretend to say yea with your lips, and annul it in your heart". Calvin traces the vice to a source that is not irreverence but unreliability: "whence is the wicked habit of swearing, except that such is the falsehood of men, that their words alone are not believed? For, if they observed faithfulness in their words, there would have been no necessity of so many superfluous oaths."
13:
Barnes rescues another word: "merry" now denotes "light and noisy pleasure", where the Greek means to have the mind well, free from trouble. Calvin takes the two clauses as covering the whole of life, since "there is no time in which God does not invite us to himself", and diagnoses the double failure they correct: "such is the perverseness of men, that they cannot rejoice without forgetting God, and that when afflicted they are disheartened and driven to despair". Robertson notes that the verb for singing meant to twang a chord. Ellicott offers Augustine's phrase for ejaculatory prayer, "arrows of the Lord's deliverance, shot out with a sudden quickness", since long petitions are not possible when mind and body are ill.

Who the elders are is settled variously. Barnes denies they can be apostles, who could not always be accessible and whose instructions were meant to be permanent, and takes them for ordinary officers. Ellicott follows Lightfoot in holding the identity of bishop and presbyter in the apostolic age "conclusive", while insisting that no reader of the Apostolic Fathers can "base on their authority any defence of Congregationalism". Calvin widens it beyond pastors to those chosen from the people "to be as it were censors to protect discipline", every church having "as it were its own senate". Barnes adds a complaint of his own: the sick are told to call for the elders, not to wait and resent the neglect — "why should they presume that their pastor will know of their illness any more than that their physician will?"

The oil divides them four ways, and each position is argued. Clarke holds it purely medicinal, his strongest reasons being that "if a miracle was intended, it could have been as well wrought without the oil", and that the text nowhere says the unction saves the sick man but that the prayer of faith does; and he notes that a rabbi anointed his sick nephew at Capernaum, who "was restored". Calvin refuses that reading in as many words — "I cannot agree with those who think that it was medicine" — and makes it a sacrament belonging to the temporary gift of healing: since the thing signified has ceased, so must the sign, and those who make anointing perpetual "are not the true followers, but the apes of the Apostles". Wesley takes the opposite view of duration: the gift "remained in the church long after the other miraculous gifts were withdrawn", indeed "seems to have been designed to remain always", and was "the whole process of physic in the Christian church, till it was lost through unbelief". Robertson holds both ends together: medicinal value attaches to the oil and weight to the prayer, and the verb may mean "rub" as in the medical writers rather than a ceremonial anointing. His conclusion is unembarrassed: "at bottom in James we have God and medicine, God and the doctor, and that is precisely where we are today. The best physicians believe in God and want the help of prayer."

On extreme unction the three who mention it agree. Calvin says the passage "is wickedly and ignorantly perverted" when used to establish it; Wesley calls it "that novel invention among the Romanists, practised not for cure, but where life is despaired of"; Robertson dates the practice after the eighth century and finds nothing of it here.

The promise of verse 15 Barnes qualifies rather than softens. Such promises carry the restriction that recovery follows if it be God's will, since taken absolutely "the sick person would always recover... and he need never die"; but he will not let that empty it, adding that "no one can demonstrate that this promise has not been in numerous instances fulfilled". On the forgiveness clause he offers two readings: that the sickness was a punishment, so healing evidences pardon, or that illness brings a past life to remembrance.
16:
The confession is read narrowly by most, and defended against one use by all. Gill confines it to "sins committed against one another", and rules out the Roman practice on two counts: that is of all sins where this is of offences between men, and that is made to priests where this is made by saints to one another. Barnes ties it to the sick man of the preceding verse, the clause adding "that ye may be healed". Wesley notes what the text does not say: "he does not say, to the elders: this may, or may not, be done; for it is nowhere commanded. We may confess them to any who can pray in faith." Robertson commends public confession in the meetings, warning that "one may confess to the pastor without confessing to God or to the church, with little benefit to anybody."

Clarke and Calvin turn the verse against it by the same reductio. Clarke: had auricular confession any foundation here "it would prove more than they wish, for it would require the priest to confess his sins to the people, as well as the people to the priest." Calvin puts it more sharply: a reciprocal confession being demanded, "no others are bidden to confess their own sins, but those who in their turn are fit to hear the confession of others". Calvin's positive reading is his own: confession is joined to prayer because "they who know our necessities, are stimulated to pray that they may assist us; but they to whom our diseases are unknown are more tardy to bring us help". Clarke gives the moral effect instead: social confession "tends much to humble the soul, and to make it watchful".

Ellicott treats the controversy historically, and evenhandedly. He quotes Alford that it "might appear astonishing, were it not notorious", that the Roman doctrine is built here, but observes that not all Catholic divines have read it so, some of the ablest admitting "that we cannot certainly affirm sacramental confession to have been meant or spoken of in this place". He then narrates the drift: open confession before the congregation was the old custom, but such plain talk "was rightly judged to be a cause of mischief to the young and innocent" and was moved to a private hearing — a change "hardly suspected of being a step in a completely new doctrine", needing centuries "to develop into the hard system of compulsory individual bondage".

On the fervency Clarke presses the participle hardest: it means "energetic supplication, or such a prayer as is suggested to the soul and wrought in it by a Divine energy", so that "the spirit of prayer is the proof that the power of God is present to heal"; Robertson reports the grammatical division: the participle is probably middle, "when it works", though Mayor argues the passive.

Elijah is chosen because he might have seemed unusable. Clarke states the difficulty: "there was some reason to apprehend that because Elijah was translated, therefore he was more than human, and if so, his example could be no pattern for us." Gill reports the rabbinic version of it, that Elijah "was not born of a father and mother, but was an angel". Barnes explains what the phrase does not mean — not that the prophet was irritable, but that "he was a mere man, subject to the same weaknesses and infirmities as other men" — and gives the reason it matters: without it the example could not encourage "the ignorant, and the weak, and children and servants". Barnes and Ellicott both notice that the Old Testament nowhere says Elijah prayed for the drought, only that he announced it; Ellicott calls the epistle's account a filling of "a lacuna in the story", and Barnes offers alternatives: that James reads the announcement as prayer "because it could be accomplished only by prayer", or reports what tradition handed down.
19:
Barnes is careful that the closing exhortation not be read as evangelism. To "convert" here "does not mean convert him as a sinner, or regenerate him, but turn him from the error of his way", and so far as the word goes the man "may have been a true Christian before". Ellicott shifts the emphasis from the erring man's will to his company: the fault is "not the wilful error, so much as the being seduced by others". He gives the rescue an image and refuses to let it finish the story: the sinner rides headlong to destruction till a friend "lays hold upon the rein, and literally converts him, i.e., turns him round; but, observe, the wanderer is still far from home, and many a weary league must he traverse before the end be neared." Henry roots the practical fault in a theoretical one: "there is some doctrinal mistake at the bottom of every practical mistake. There is no one habitually bad, but upon some bad principle."

Whose soul is saved is verse 20's first question; Barnes settles it against the manuscripts he reports. Several copies and versions read "his soul", but the natural sense is the soul of the one converted, "since it is nowhere else taught that the method of saving our souls is by converting others". The death intended must be eternal, "for the apostle cannot mean that he would save the soul from annihilation, for it is in no danger of that". Calvin states the responsibility carefully: "we must take heed lest souls perish through our sloth, whose salvation God puts in a manner in our hands. Not that we can bestow salvation on them; but that God by our ministry delivers those who seem otherwise nigh destruction." Wesley says the same in a line, of how much more value the soul is.

Whose sins are covered is the sharper question, and Clarke attacks one answer with heat. Many take the covering to be of the converter's own sins: "this is a dangerous doctrine, and what the Holy Spirit never taught to man", since it would set men to reforming neighbours in order to keep their own beloved sins. He names Bishop Atterbury and Scott for holding that the pious action "engages God to look with greater indulgence on the character of the person that performs it", calls it "doubly dangerous" and "completely antievangelical" — "if one pious act can procure pardon for a multitude of sins, what may not be expected from many?" — and adds that the Jewish teaching was sounder, rewarding the act but never letting it atone.

Robertson reports the division without heat: the Roman Catholics, and also Mayor and Ropes, take it of the converter's sins, "who thus saves himself by saving others", and "the language here will allow that, but not New Testament teaching in general". He traces the phrase to Proverbs and Peter, where it plainly covers others' sins. Ellicott says flatly "not, of course, his own, but those of the penitent". Calvin claims more for James than for Solomon, whose love buries sins as to men: "James teaches here something higher, that is, that sins are blotted out before God". Henry reaches the same end more plainly — "there is no way effectually and finally to hide sin, but forsaking it" — and closes on the supply: "for six thousand years He has been multiplying pardons, and yet his free grace is not tired."

Ellicott ends on the writer: what James was in word "that also was he in deed", since he prayed for the men who killed him — "'Hold,' said some of the by-standers, when the martyr sank upon the stones, 'the Just is praying for you!'" And he draws the inference: "Stephen's prayer won Saul for the infant Church: it can hardly be that James's last breathings of pity were unanswered of God."
